title: An SNL Sketch That Understands How the Internet Shapes Our Reality
excerpt: Sharing the culture you love—a beloved song, that book that changed your life—can help translate your inner world to the people you love
body: Sharing the culture you love—a beloved song, that book that changed your life—can help translate your inner world to the people you love

So it goes in one sketch from last night’s Saturday Night Live , in which a trio of teen girls at a sleepover (played by Sarah Sherman, Veronika Slowikowska, and Jane Wickline) take turns playing clips of their favorite get-ready-with-me videos, the popular format where content creators dress and prepare themselves for the day ahead

Two of the girls share par-for-the-course videos, before Sherman’s character introduces everyone to the influencer she loves the most: @ColoradoVicky1 (Dakota Johnson, the show’s host), a woman whose life doesn’t seem so aspirational

As she smiles cheerfully, her eyes vacant, Vicky invites her audience to “get ready with me for court-ordered electroshock therapy.” In another clip, she styles herself in green lipstick and a Teletubby-esque antenna in preparation for getting “5150’d on the roof of a San Bernardino Whole Foods.” “She seems … unwell,” says Slowikowska’s character

But Sherman’s teen girl pays no mind to such judgments, or to her friend’s question about how she found this account, whose videos don’t even have double-digit views. “I’m legiterally addicted to her ass,” Sherman says. “Guess my algorithm is just cool-mazing?!” These days, everyone uses a different internet

Algorithms serve up specialized content catered to each user’s unique interests, creating a warped mirror of their own reality, and last night’s sketch cleverly captured the disconnect that sometimes arises when people reveal their private online consumption to one another. @ColoradoVicky1’s behavior only gets more bizarre the more clips the girls watch
Without blinking once, Vicky explains that her “outfit of the day” is a pair of handcuffs, which she plans to use to attach herself to the actor who plays Turtle in Entourage

She one-ups this proclamation with an even stranger how-to video, in which she asks viewers to tag along as she makes brunch and gives herself a lobotomy. (“You’re gonna want to start by finding a really good power drill,” she monotones.) [ Read: The loneliness crisis hits SNL ] Sherman’s friends seem to get progressively more put off by her media diet
It doesn’t help that Sherman’s character isn’t the only one in the house who could probably stand to log off

Every few minutes, her dad (James Austin Johnson) comes into the room with snacks and immediately reveals how depressed he is: “I’m just gonna go drink in the pool for a while, stand in the deep end,” he announces, before leaving the room
When the sleepover guests are concerned, Sherman explains that her dad is just in a funk: His boss discovered he dresses up like Sailor Moon, and he just found out that Draft Kings uses real money
His particular online milieu is bleeding into, and beginning to harm, his real-life existence

When her friends ask if they should get help, Sherman’s character insists that they “stop giving him attention—that’s, like, exactly what he wants.” She continues to ignore his not-so-subtle cries for help, until the sketch’s ending beat, in which he randomly shows up in @ColoradoVicky1’s livestream as her new lover
Sherman seems thrilled by this development, announcing that Vicky is going to be her new mom
Finally, her father’s real-life depression is good for something
Teen girls and their dads alike are vulnerable to having their minds and lives warped by their feeds, the sketch warns

And once brought to light, these online rabbit holes might not translate so well to real life: The sketch-comedy version of this is funny because it’s so familiar, while the fracturing of reality outside SNL is mostly just unnerving.

title: Puffins
excerpt: The wind brings the circus to a lonesome town upstate, and puffins to the Isle of May, seagirt, desolate
body: The wind brings the circus to a lonesome town upstate, and puffins to the Isle of May, seagirt, desolate
The wind brings spectators by ferry to the docks
Side by side like gravy boats seals loll on the rocks
The throng swipes their shoes on a disinfectant mat, running down the gangplank to the puffins’ habitat
The main ring is the breeding ground where lies their single egg circled with a constant cry echoed off the crag
They circle, circle, swoop, and dive, coming back with silver sprats like spiny roses in the teeth of undefeated acrobats
The comic masks they wear belie the effort it must take to migrate all their lives in search of a decent windbreak
Clown-bright lichen clothes the rocks, sea campion froths in grass
Here’s the roofless abbey on a speck in the atlas
This poem appears in the November 2026 print edition.

title: AI’s Real Gift to Science
excerpt: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has often said that AI will cure most diseases in the next 10 years
body: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has often said that AI will cure most diseases in the next 10 years

Late last month, he claimed that his company had taken a first step toward that future: Claude had, in less than 24 hours, discovered a new “enzyme system” that the company says resembles CRISPR, a gene-editing tool currently curing people of diseases

While announcing the discovery, Anthropic hinted that this was the type of finding that revolutionizes medicine and quoted a gene-editing pioneer who called it “genuinely intriguing.” The company was open about not knowing what exactly it had spotted or whether the finding—the first released from a biology lab that the company established this spring—was really that significant
Still, many academics, along with the CEO of Eli Lilly, pointed out that the company had dressed up a very incremental finding as a major discovery
Fyodor Urnov, a scientist who coined the term genome editing and is working on a CRISPR project with Anthropic, told me that “the jury is out” on whether what Claude found is even an enzyme at all

Multiple researchers told The New York Times that, in fact, they had been aware of the supposedly new enzyme system for years, including a team at the University of Copenhagen that alleged Anthropic’s new results might have been stolen from their lab’s interactions with Claude

The company, in response, said that Claude isn’t trained using user transcripts. (Anthropic did not respond to a comment request for this article.) In other words, Anthropic made a big deal about a finding that—although achieved in a novel, Claude-led way—may not lead to any biomedical advances, and that the company knew may not lead to any biomedical advances

Ironically, in making such grandiose statements, the company and other AI boosters obscured what Claude does appear to have accomplished: It sorted through reams of biological data that would have taken scientists much longer to analyze, if they could have at all
This capacity might not be a miracle, but for scientists facing mountains of data that have surpassed their capacity for analysis, it’s still meaningful
Around the turn of the 21st century, researchers sequenced for the first time all 3 billion letters that make up human DNA
This effort, called the Human Genome Project, took 13 years and cost $2.7 billion
Today, sequencing a person’s full genome takes just over a day and costs as little as $200
Accordingly, the total amount of publicly available genomic data has become so large as to be unmanageable
In other fields, such as protein science, technological advances have led to a similar boom in the sheer amount of data being collected
Trying to pull anything useful from all that data has become its own long-term project

In 2012, a committee of bioinformatics experts found that the “bottleneck in scientific productivity” had moved from data production to data analysis, but early efforts at the National Institutes of Health to deal with that bottleneck quickly sputtered out

If researchers could efficiently store, send, and examine all of the information they generated, they would likely be able to, for example, develop new drugs by identifying better genes or cellular parts to target
But it’s simply too massive for them to comprehensively attack
The biological corpus is not, however, too large for AI agents

Bo Wang, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto and the chief AI scientist at a drug-discovery company, recently wrote that AI’s biggest impact in biology will come from its help “scaling scientific attention”: Setting agents loose on the enormous data sets can surface the outliers that warrant further human inspection

Agents can propose and test hypotheses for what might cause the unusual patterns they find, and predictive modeling can help scientists choose what experiments to carry out on their actual lab benches
Eventually, automated labs might even carry out those chosen experiments—a few already exist in the United States, and the Trump administration is spending hundreds of millions to establish more
Meanwhile, scientists remain divided over whether AI models actually steer them toward potentially paradigm-shifting experiments, or safer, less exploratory ones

AI is already changing medicine: Models that use people’s medical history to predict their health risks, including their likelihood of developing certain kinds of cancer, are now used in most U.S. hospitals
At the same time, not every field of biology generates enough data for this approach to work

AI might be less useful in some domains that rely on less abundant microscopy data, such as the study of how cells and tissues communicate; such data tend to be harder to come by than genetic sequences, Stirling Churchman, a professor of genetics at Harvard Medical School, told me
Organelle biology and the science of cellular transport similarly require painstaking, time-consuming experiments
Still, Churchman said, “there will be magic where there’s data.” She spent the summer at OpenAI working on a specially trained model for life-science researchers

She anticipates that by allowing scientists who can’t code to examine their data themselves, AI will enable researchers to “analyze data at least 10 times faster, freeing us to spend more time on the biological questions and experiments.” The recent Anthropic finding is an example of how AI can identify outliers that might otherwise have gone unnoticed
Existing tools can comb through heaps of genomic data (and have already been used to identify bona fide new gene-editing systems)

What AI can do is run those kinds of analyses at a much larger scale, while also evaluating intermediary results, Kendell Clement, who runs a computational-biology lab at the University of Utah, told me
Of course, that scale requires dumping in correspondingly huge resources: Anthropic directed about 950 Claude bots to simultaneously pore over a database that contained nearly 2 billion DNA entries
AI companies have every incentive to keep evangelizing about the medical miracles they say their models will unlock, especially as backlash against them mounts
Amodei has an idea for how to quiet AI skeptics: “The thing that will work is actually curing cancer,” he recently wrote on X
But helping scientists work more quickly is, too, even if it doesn’t sound quite so revolutionary.

title: The Vanity of Kings
excerpt: Not so long ago , heroic public statuary felt irrelevant—good for locating yourself in traffic circles but otherwise dismissed as a relic of some credulous, gre
body: Not so long ago , heroic public statuary felt irrelevant—good for locating yourself in traffic circles but otherwise dismissed as a relic of some credulous, great-man-besotted past
The fact that places like Pyongyang and Ashgabat still went in for it just confirmed the association with autocratic backwardness and childish megalomania

In Washington, D.C., millions of taxpayer dollars were spent on regilding a pair of allegorical equestrian bronzes with the cheap sheen of a dollar-store trophy, and the Trump administration has been defiantly pursuing legally contested plans for an arch of hypertrophic vulgarity

Meanwhile, in Los Angeles, an exhibition with Kara Walker’s dismembered and reconstituted statue of Stonewall Jackson and his horse became one of the most widely covered art events of the past 12 months
Figurative monuments are now being taken seriously—desired by some (well, at least one guy), vilified by many, and argued over by just about everybody

Whose history do they tell? When should they be pulled down or repurposed? How effective are they anyway? In this environment, the advent of two big museum shows with “Pharaohs” in the title feels timely
No people on Earth have done monuments more ambitiously and lastingly than the ancient Egyptians

Staking claims to eternal fame, pharaohs stamped their names and features on objects of mind-boggling scale: the Great Sphinx of Giza, the Colossi of Memnon, the mountainous figures of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel

Curated by the former director of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, Tarek el-Awady, and with a catalog by the high-profile Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass, “ Treasures of the Pharaohs ” is both a buzzy blockbuster and an assiduous cultural survey. (Now at the de Young Museum, in San Francisco, it will travel to the Kimbell Art Museum, in Fort Worth, next year.) Its 100-plus artifacts stretch from tiny gold animal amulets some 5,000 years old to a gilded incense burner about 2,700 years younger, and from a child’s clay rattle found in a workers’ settlement near Thebes to the gold funerary mask of the 21st-dynasty king Amenemope, his bland face framed by the flanged nemes headdress still de rigueur for all costume-party pharaohs

Styles changed over that enormous time span: The French-bob wig shown on a statue of Lady Hekenu in the fifth dynasty differs from the Gidget flips worn by Ukh-Hotep’s wives in the 12th dynasty, which look nothing like the elaborate braided wigs of Senetnay and her daughter in the 18th dynasty

Wigs aside, however, the story is one of overarching continuity: a society structured around divine kingship, detailed preparations for the afterlife, and the cosmological ideal of truth, justice, and order known as ma’at , all of which found expression in a remarkably stable set of visual forms
New pharaohs imitated the monuments of old pharaohs or had them retailored to fit themselves

The essential Egyptian pictorial convention of figures in profile with torsos twisted forward was already in place by the time of King Narmer (around 3000 B.C.E.) and was still serving Cleopatra in 30 B.C.E. (It’s worth noting that the distance between those two rulers is 1,000 years longer than that between Cleopatra and us.) The hook is Bronze Age glamour, and exhibition publicity gives pride of place to the beautiful golden face and blue-lined eyes of Thuya, mother-in-law of the pharaoh Amenhotep III

But Hawass also wants viewers to understand Egypt as “a pioneering power that demonstrated how to build a unified state, establishing the fundamental principles of science and governance.” A model boat from the early Middle Kingdom (circa 2000 B.C.E.), fully staffed with oarsmen, a captain, and a sailor plumbing the depths, serves a discussion of Egyptian nautical sophistication
Tomb portraits of commoners such as the carpenter Inty‑Shedu back up Hawass’s claim that Egypt’s social stability rested in part on its allowance for skill-based upward mobility
The problem for big surveys like “Treasures” is that it’s hard to keep track of so many pharaohs, dynasties, kingdoms, and gods (Hawass counts more than 1,500 deities)

The larger sociological points land, and many objects dazzle, but the individual biographies tend to blur. “Maverick Kings: Three Visionary Pharaohs of Egypt’s Golden Age,” at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, takes a different approach
Berman, the exhibit’s curator, has written two books that tease out tales of individual lives from objects in his care
This exhibition does something similar, zeroing in on Hatshepsut, Amenhotep III (him again), and his son Akhenaten
All belonged to the 18th dynasty (circa 1550–1292 B.C.E.), when Egypt was at its richest and most self-assured
All were outliers in different ways, and all were committed (it’s tempting to say addicted) to proclaiming their achievements and broadcasting their images as broadly as possible

The daughter of one pharaoh and the half sister and wife of another (a frequent Egyptian arrangement), Hatshepsut was serving as co-regent with her young nephew/stepson when she took the title of king herself—an extraordinary, though not unprecedented, action
For more than two decades, she kept the peace, expanded trade, and transformed the temple complex of Karnak at Thebes
She aggrandized processional routes with monuments, including obelisks of solid granite that rose 100 feet and were topped with electrum (a mirror-bright natural gold-silver alloy)
Built into the cliffs on the west bank of the Nile, her memorial temple rises in stepped terraces, like something Frank Lloyd Wright might have done if he’d had the power and purse of a potentate
These efforts may have been for the glory of the dynasty’s official state god, Amun‑Re, but statues of Hatshepsut punctuated the vistas like a visual drumbeat
The Metropolitan Museum of Art A delicately feminine statue of Hatshepsut, a rare woman who took the title of king
In Boston, an obelisk fragment shows Hatshepsut flat-chested and broad-shouldered, wearing the kilt, headdress, and rectangular false beard of a pharaoh
But in a beguiling seated statue on loan from the Metropolitan Museum of Art, she appears distinctly feminine, delicate and beardless, though still clad in a pharaoh’s kilt and headdress
These variations tell us less about Hatshepsut’s gender proclivities than about monuments as public performance
Egyptian kingship had a recognized visual grammar, and attributes of office could operate independently of physiognomic truth
A manly statue of Hatshepsut was no different in principle from the perennially youthful Ramesses II we see depicted across his six and a half decades on the throne
Amenhotep III was Hatshepsut’s great-great-grandnephew and perhaps “the greatest patron of the arts in Egypt’s history,” Berman writes

Having inherited a kingdom and immense wealth, he threw himself into aggrandizing old temples and constructing new ones; he built a palace complex big enough to accommodate an artificial lake and accessorized everything with statues of himself, including the 60-foot-tall Colossi of Memnon
Tempering the geometric rigor of earlier monuments with a new sensuality of form, he established an Egyptian classicism to which later generations repeatedly returned
It’s hard, looking at the finely carved quartzite head of Amenhotep in Boston, to grasp the majesty it would once have conveyed
His skull flows into the bowling-pin-shaped crown of Upper Egypt in a way that closely resembles the Coneheads of early SNL
And whereas most pharaohs are shown with a small, serene smile, Amenhotep’s heavy-lidded eyes, elegant brows, and grinning lips convey such self-satisfied beatitude that he looks a bit stoned
Originally, however, the head was probably part of a standing statue in which the king’s living spirit was present
Instead of conveying drowsiness, those lowered eyelids would have directed his gaze down at subjects, who would have felt themselves seen by a king and a god

title: Should We Ban AI for Kids?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Long before he became famous as the author of The Anxious Generation , Jonathan Haidt was a social psychologi
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Long before he became famous as the author of The Anxious Generation , Jonathan Haidt was a social psychologist whose work revolutionized the field

In this episode of The Permanent Questions , taped in front of a live audience at last month’s Atlantic Festival, David Brooks talks with Haidt about his biggest lessons from 40 years of studying human nature

David and Haidt discuss the role of the emotions in moral decision making, how to design a system that produces less loathsome elites, and why AI is “the neutron bomb for education.” The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Today we’re joined by Jonathan Haidt, who is a social psychologist at New York University, and these days he’s best known for The Anxious Generation , a book on what the phones are doing to our kids
That book has sold eight zillion copies, but more importantly, it’s launched a social movement, which Jonathan is leading, to get phones out of schools
It’s been a phenomenally successful social movement

I get to visit high schools, maybe a dozen a year, and every one I go to has either banned phones from schools or is in the process of working out some arrangement to reduce the access to phones in schools
Everywhere I go, the kids love it, the teachers love it
It’s having a huge positive effect on our schools
When we first became friends, he was working as a social psychologist at the University of Virginia, and I was a baby pundit
And over the last 40 years, Jonathan has observed and also taken part in what you might call an intellectual revolution
We have learned so much because of his field, social psychology, because of neuroscience, because of cognitive psychology, because of a whole range of fields
We have learned so much about human nature
So for this conversation, I wanted to step back from the phones—though we’ll touch on that—and ask the big question
We’ve learned a lot about human nature over the last 30 or 40 years

What’s important here? What are the key things we should understand about what human beings are and how we work? I think this is an urgent question, because every system we have in society—whether it’s our economic system, our political system, our school system—all of them are based on a certain set of assumptions about human nature
If those assumptions turn out to be wrong, then we’re creating systems that will deform and mutilate the people within them
One more thing you should know about this conversation
This one was recorded in September at The Atlantic Festival in New York City, in front of a live audience
I was thrilled to welcome Jonathan Haidt to The Permanent Questions
We’ve known each other for a while, and I had the chance to go back and look over your oeuvre
Jonathan Haidt: My oeuvre. ( Laughs .) Brooks: Or “Hoover,” as we say in New York
I read The Happiness Hypothesis , which is 20 years old now, coming out again, and I developed a theory that people don’t start out as bad writers of books and then grow into good writers of books
They start out as good writers of books and keep going
Then you wrote The Righteous Mind , which was an important contribution to moral psychology, a very important contribution—re-shifted the whole field, basically

Then you got into The Coddling of the American Mind , and then you wrote The Anxious Generation about phones, which not only changed America—I go to schools all the time with no phones in them, and the kids love them, without exception—it also sold a zillion copies
So it is a sign of what a wonderful human being I am that I am not consumed with envy and jealousy at this moment
So we’ll start with technology, and then we’re gonna move off to wider psychology

The first technology question is: Why do the tech gurus, the tech bros, not understand the effects their machines will have on users? Haidt: First, I just want to say what a pleasure it is to be here with you
As we got to know each other, I’ve always felt that we have very similar brains
We just started at different points, and then we ended up kind of converging on psychology and politics and flourishing
Also, we were both very ambitious workaholics who were super cerebral, which is related to what we’re about to talk about
But then somewhere along the line, we began to get a little more humanistic
All of us have been watching David from the beginning
The change— Brooks: I had a lot of fertilizer inside to work with
Haidt: My point is I think we’re both people who might have once been the sort who would become rationalists, but we didn’t
In preparing for this, I went back to my book The Righteous Mind , and I have a whole chapter on rationalism

It turns out rationalism is kind of the negative force of the entire book, because rationalism has dominated moral philosophy and moral thinking since Plato, through Kant, Bentham— Brooks: Why don’t you define what you mean by “rationalism”? Haidt: It’s the idea that there are moral truths that can be known, and the way that you know them is by thinking, logic, reasoning
That works pretty well for mathematical truths
But the debate in moral philosophy was really brought in by David Hume, who said: No, look at the way reason works
Reason is, and ought only to be, the servant of the passions

title: Are Mormons Losing Their Distinctiveness?
excerpt: Mormons have sometimes called themselves a “ peculiar people ,” and statistically, they have been
body: Mormons have sometimes called themselves a “ peculiar people ,” and statistically, they have been
Compared with Protestants, Catholics, Jews, and Buddhists, Latter-day Saints have higher birth rates , higher marriage rates , and larger families
They also have a relatively high retention rate—meaning that those who are born into the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints tend to stay members for life
But recently, all of these long-held patterns have started to shift
The Church is not facing a crisis, exactly—more of a demographic ravine than a cliff, Jana Riess, a historian who studies the LDS faith, told me
But as of 2024 , only about half of young people born into the Church stay in it—down from more than 80 percent in the 1980s

Its marriage rate has fallen 10 percent since 2011, and in the past 40 years, the number of annual recorded births per 1,000 LDS members has dropped from 25 to five, according to an analysis of Church records by the independent data scientist Alex Bass
If Latter-day Saints’ peculiarity was defined in part by their early marriages, their minivans full of kids, and their loyalty to the Church, some of that peculiarity seems to be slipping away
The LDS Church’s birth-rate and retention problems are far from unique: People in the United States are having fewer babies and leaving religion pretty much across the board

Doug Andersen, a spokesperson for the Church, wrote to me in an email that “official church records show consistent worldwide increases in both membership and participation,” in part because a record number of converts are joining worldwide
Still, the demographic tilt is enough of a problem that the Church’s new leader, Dallin Oaks, is taking notice
Under the previous Church prophet, mentions of family were fewer and farther between at the Church’s biannual conference

But this year, in his first conference address since becoming prophet, Oaks issued a warning: Although the Church’s marriage and birth rates were better than the U.S. average, they had declined significantly. “We are a family Church,” he said , and quoted from the 1995 “Family Proclamation,” which once hung on the walls of many LDS homes: “God’s commandment for His children to multiply and replenish the earth remains in force.” In some ways, what’s happening to the LDS now is what happens to any religion that grows beyond a core of strong believers

Over time, the more particular edges of a faith—the meatless Fridays of Catholicism, for instance—can get sanded down until it more closely resembles mainstream American culture and mainline Protestantism, Matthew Bowman, the chair of Mormon Studies at Claremont Graduate University, told me. (The Church now discourages use of the word “Mormon” as a nickname for members of the faith, but the term is still used in proper names, such as Bowman’s title or The Book of Mormon.) To him, the demographic shifts in the LDS indicate that “the long process of assimilation is becoming more noticeable now.” Compared with individual Protestant denominations, such as Methodism, the LDS looks like it’s doing better at retaining its young people, Justin Dyer, a religion professor at Brigham Young University, told me
But Ryan Burge, a political scientist at Washington University in St
Louis, argues that that’s not the right comparison to make, because even if someone switches from Methodist to Lutheran, they still hold pretty much the same Protestant beliefs
And Protestantism’s retention more generally, at 70 percent, far surpasses the LDS Church’s
Lower retention may also have more ramifications for the LDS Church than it would for Methodists
Fewer young people means fewer missionaries
And fewer members means that the work of operating churches, which are volunteer-led at the local and regional levels, will fall on fewer people

In the past, the Church’s robust structure for kids (Sunday school, youth programs, regional dances, and sleepaway camps) carried young people into missionary work, which usually equated to lifelong membership, but that formula seems to be failing now, Jana Riess said. (She herself is an LDS member.) “The Church has been great at retention in the past and is doing many of the same things that used to be so successful then
So it’s understandable why leaders would be sort of wringing their hands and saying, ‘Why isn’t this enough?’” The Church is having a particularly hard time keeping young women
In 2025, fewer than 40 percent of 18-year-old girls stayed in the faith, according to Dyer’s research

Many apostates leave because they are more liberal than the Church on issues such as same-sex marriage, but when Riess interviewed young women for her upcoming book on people who leave the faith, many of them also brought up feeling undervalued by the Church

In LDS theology, only men can hold what is called the priesthood—the authority given by God to Joseph Smith and passed down through every generation of LDS men—which allows them to bless children and the sick, pass the sacrament, and serve in certain leadership positions

Because of this, essentially, “there is nowhere in the LDS Church where a man reports to a woman on questions of final authority, and there is nowhere in the LDS Church where a woman has final say,” Bowman said

And the 1995 Family Proclamation made clear that a wife’s role is to nurture the children. “It’s a tough position for the Church to be in,” Riess said. “It wants to remain attractive to women in a culture that has moved in a different direction, but also wants to stay pretty much on the same path of emphasizing this very particular configuration of the nuclear family.” Many women do not mind the Church’s male priesthood, or at least accept it. “I can believe that something’s divine but also fallible at the same time,” Sophie Smith, a graduate student at BYU, told me

She believes that women already have many ways to contribute to the faith and that “whether it’s in this life or the next, it will not be a patriarchal Church.” But LDS leaders do seem to be aware of the Church’s young-women problem: Women can now direct their ward’s Sunday-school program, and recently, the Church lowered the age at which women can serve a mission from 19 to 18

This decision has led to a record boom in missionary numbers, but it’s also “a way to keep young women in the fold and try to socialize them more deeply in the faith,” Riess said. (One refrain in LDS circles, Bowman said, is: “A missionary’s most important convert is himself or herself.”) Completing a mission at 18 also means that young women can get married sooner: They return around age 20, and “on the LDS checklist, the next check is getting married and having children,” Alyssa Beck, who leads classes for teenage girls at her ward in Los Angeles, told me
Women who do lean into the Church’s call to motherhood may still struggle to have a big family, though
Smith has noticed those around her having fewer kids, mostly because they can’t afford more

For years, the single-family-home price in the so-called Mormon Corridor—Utah, Idaho, and Arizona—ran below the national average, but since 2020, prices have soared above that threshold, according to Bass’s analysis . “There are still people who are like, I wanna have eight kids , and that’s awesome,” Smith said
But out of necessity—because both parents need to work, and kids are expensive—many don’t
These younger families may find less than they once did to keep them immersed in the culture of the religion

Between bazaars, choirs, plays, and road shows , congregants might have once been at their chapel four times a week; now many active members come only on Sundays, Bowman said. (And even Sunday services have been shortened from three hours to two.) As the faith has grown internationally, “the cultural apparatus that was built in Utah just wasn’t exportable,” Bowman said, and because the Church tries to keep its practices consistent across the world (whether in Kenya or Utah, every chapel uses the same teachings and Sunday-school curriculum), he believes that Church leadership pared back the social expectations of being a Latter-day Saint

That cultural loosening might be helping the Church grow internationally and simultaneously making it easier for American members to leave. (Andersen, the LDS spokesperson, said that the Church is “encouraged by increased participation of our children, youth, and young adults in the United States in the past decade.”) For now, the Church seems to be insisting that its future is rooted in family—which will require people to heed the words of the prophet, and multiply and replenish the Earth
To do that, though, young people will need to stick around

Churches across the country, not just the LDS, are trying to figure out that particular puzzle: Recently, many younger Americans have passionately recommitted to religion, but their depth of feeling hasn’t caught on widely —at least not yet
Whether they grew up LDS, Catholic, or Baptist, many Americans seem to want churches to offer some combination of retreat from mainstream U.S. life and assimilation in it
But, as Bowman said, “that is a very, very tricky sweet spot to hit.”

title: When does trying to have a healthier baby become eugenics-y?
excerpt: Editor’s note, October 4, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave
body: Editor’s note, October 4, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave
The one below was originally published last year
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
My partner and I did IVF recently and luckily we ended up with several embryos
One of those will be implanted in me so I hopefully get pregnant

But which one? My fertility clinic is encouraging me to do PGT-A testing, which would screen for things like Down syndrome and would also let me see the sex of each embryo so I could potentially choose whichever I want. (And to be honest, I really want a girl!) I’m also hearing about these new companies that can test embryos for all kinds of things — like how smart the kid might be, how tall they’ll get, and whether they’ll have a lower chance of getting breast cancer, diabetes, mental illness, stuff like that
I don’t know how to feel about any of this
On the one hand, it feels weirdly eugenics-y to do so much tinkering with embryos, and I can’t help feeling a little pressured into overmedicalizing everything with these expensive tests

But then again, if I could do something to make my baby healthier and happier, don’t I kind of have to do everything in my power? What does a parent owe their child? Dear Expecting, This is such an exciting — and also confusing — time
You’re about to have your first kid, and that comes with all sorts of fears and insecurities and hopes and dreams
You want to do the right thing — no, the best thing! — for your child
Unfortunately, it makes it easy for companies to prey on you
So let me walk you through what these companies can and can’t really provide
After we talk about the science, we can talk about the ethics.  The simpler test you mentioned, PGT-A, has been around since the 1990s
It can indeed screen for conditions like Down syndrome and let you see the sex of each embryo
Mind you, that doesn’t predict what gender your child will ultimately end up identifying with — more on that soon
The newer testing you mentioned is called polygenic testing
The conditions it screens for are complex ones, influenced by thousands of genes
We’re talking about everything from breast cancer to depression
Some companies even offer screenings not for disease prevention, but for genetic enhancement — so you can select for a taller kid or a kid with higher IQ
Polygenic testing companies claim to predict each embryo’s risk for each condition, and the potential reduction of risk you’ll get if you choose one embryo over another
As the statistical geneticist Sasha Gusev explains , it’s very, very easy to be misled by this claim

If the company claims to lower absolute risk of Type 2 diabetes by 12 percent, you might think this means, “The chance of my kid ever developing diabetes just went down by 12 percent — great!” But really what it means is that, all else equal, a kid who would’ve developed diabetes is likely now at the high end of pre-diabetes instead, or just develops diabetes a few years later
The same holds true for other conditions, like breast cancer

Sure, if your kid is going to develop diabetes or breast cancer, you’d rather they develop it later — but it’s not the bill of perfect health customers might imagine. “Typical risk reduction estimates tend to exploit statistical assumptions to overstate their benefits and lead to confusion,” Gusev writes

Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions

Sign up here! It’s also important to note that there’s a difference between a physical disease like cancer, which is straightforwardly and universally negative, and a complex mental health condition like depression
For one thing, polygenic scores don’t perform as well in psychiatry , as the psychologist Eric Turkheimer notes

Plus, most mental health conditions come in mild to moderate to severe forms, and it’s not clear that we should want to get rid of mild or moderate manifestations. “Sure, it would be nice if no one ever got depressed, but what would that actually mean?” Turkheimer writes. “People are going to be sad, and the most modern models of psychiatric disorders view most of them as extremes on continuous dimensions of normal behavior
I don’t think we want some kind of genetic version of Soma .” To give a personal example: I have generalized anxiety with some obsessive tendencies
Is that a major pain in the butt sometimes? You bet
But if I could wave a magic wand and get rid of it, would I? No
In my experience, this trait is linked to another trait I deeply value: my creativity

The same thing that propels me down rabbit holes of worry also propels me down rabbit holes of getting super curious about some topic, researching it into the wee hours of the morning, and then writing a novel or children’s book about it
That brings me to one other scientific issue: pleiotropy
It’s a fancy term for a simple truth, which is that genes can have an effect on more than one trait

When it comes to behavioral polygenic testing, we actually know very little about which genes cause what — a gene that’s correlated with depression or anxiety may also be correlated with a bunch of other things

So, if everyone were to start selecting embryos to try to protect their kids from depression or anxiety, what would happen? We don’t know!  Pleiotropy is a scientific issue, but it’s also a moral issue, because in trying to protect your kid from a negative outcome, you could also be accidentally barring them from a positive one
And that’s just the tip of the moral iceberg

title: Can thrift shops save us from Shein?
excerpt: Think about what you’re wearing right now
body: Think about what you’re wearing right now
Did you pick it out? Or was it chosen for you by an algorithm you haven’t even considered?  You may think it’s the former, but with the state of the fashion industry, it’s likely the latter

There was a time when taste was decided by designers at luxury fashion houses, à la Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel, or Anna Wintour-type magazine editors (think of the famous cerulean sweater monologue from The Devil Wears Prada )
Now, in the era of fast fashion, our clothing options are often dictated by computers.  Amy Odell writes the Back Row newsletter and hosts a podcast with the same name

She told Vox that what’s known as fast fashion has been kicked into hyperdrive by companies like Shein.  “I’ve also heard it called instant fashion,” she says. “The way it works is that they use algorithms to track trends and what people are interested in, and then they make a few hundred of a very large number of different items and they test demand.” She says this model has allowed companies like Shein to introduce around 4,700 new apparel styles per day. (For comparison, fast fashion brand Zara produces around 20,000 a year.) Some are trying to claw back their personal style by hitting the thrift store instead
Traditionally, it’s where people go to find less expensive clothes

But fashion journalist Hannah Marriott says it can be so much more than that.  “For the last probably a hundred years, [the thrift store] has had lots of moments where it’s been cool within countercultures,” Marriott told Vox. “Whether it’s grunge, or the surrealists in the 1920s, or the Rolling Stones in the 1960s, secondhand clothing was cool because of the stigma.”  So how did thrifting go from stigmatized to chic? And are thrift stores still thrifty now that they’re more mainstream, especially in an era of ultra-cheap Shein clothing? We find out that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Marriott, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
There’s sometimes this stigma that’s attached to buying secondhand clothes
How has its perception changed over time? Secondhand clothing used to be something that there was a real sense that if you couldn’t buy new, you would buy secondhand

At the same time, it has had lots of moments where it’s been cool within countercultures.  People within countercultures — whether it’s grunge, or the surrealists in the 1920s, or the Rolling Stones in the 1960s — secondhand clothing was cool because of the stigma

It’s also been a really important resource for people on lower incomes for a long time.  I think it was a gradual shift by various things that happened in the pandemic, including this absolute influx of apps [like The RealReal and Depop] that got very, very popular during that time, particularly among younger Gen Z consumers
Thrifting became a social currency on social media platforms, especially on TikTok
It’s a vast ecosystem at the moment, and all of them have slightly different business models, slightly different fees that they charge, and slightly different audiences that they’re reaching
The stigma has really gone away, and it’s almost reversed
What does that ecosystem look like? There are different layers to it
There are consignment places like The RealReal where they take quite a big cut, but they will promote your items for you
I think those sites tend to work best if you’ve actually got designer clothes that have quite a big margin, particularly handbags
Then there are other sites that are a bit more laid-back: eBay maybe skews a bit older, Depop skews a bit younger and trendier
There’s Vinted, which I know from the UK, but is making inroads into the US now

It’s an absolutely vast ecosystem at the moment, and all of them have slightly different business models, slightly different fees that they charge, and slightly different audiences that they’re reaching
One of the biggest secondhand shops here in the US is still Goodwill
Can you walk me through how Goodwill has adapted and changed to the secondhand boom? Neighborhood thrift stores of that kind are the sort of stores that people on lower incomes do rely on more
It’s less trend-led than something like Depop
And it is somewhere that people have often been going for decades to get clothes that they can afford.  Goodwill undeniably has put its prices up

Inflation is such an issue for everyone, so I’m sure that there would be an element of prices going up anyway, but a lot of shoppers feel strongly that they’ve gone up a lot — that you can’t find bargains anymore, that the bargains get sent online to either their website or are bought by resellers who sell them for an inflated price online.  It’s hard to get to the bottom of exactly how true all of that is, especially because Goodwill is run as 150 autonomous [nonprofits], and each of them set their own prices

But what I would say is you are seeing things like the Goodwill branch in Connecticut charging $75 bucks to go on a thrift tour coach to get early access to a Goodwill store, and then you get to go to another store
You used to be able to buy 10 things in Goodwill for $75
It’s so interesting that thrifting used to be this edgy original thing, but it’s really gone mainstream

Has it sold out?   I remember when I was much younger, people would say, “Ooh, you got that secondhand.” I just don’t think anyone would ever say that now because that’s kind of how we shop.  But I still think it is great if you find something original that you love that no one else has, and I still think you’re more likely to find it secondhand or in certain other under-the-radar brands that aren’t fast fashion.  I think maybe this is a reaction to 30 years of fast fashion just getting faster and faster and faster
I think we’re all feeling a bit tired of that business model, so we’re trying to find other ways to shop and express ourselves.

title: Hunter-gatherer societies are often put on a pedestal as paragons of equality – but the reality is more complicated
url:
<title>Hunter-gatherer societies are often put on a pedestal as paragons of equality – but the reality is more complicated</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763725/original/file-20261002-60-8lnm30.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C618%2C3680%2C2453&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Even in egalitarian societies, people can be unequal in various ways.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Duncan Stibbard Hawkes</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal – a <a href="https://www.britannica.com/animal/kudu">kudu</a>. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas and heads home to enlist help.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="head of a horned, deer-like animal with pieces of its carcass" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=937&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=937&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=937&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1178&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1178&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763721/original/file-20261002-50-ysegy4.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1178&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A kudu post-butchering, with portions going to various community members.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Duncan Stibbard Hawkes</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>News spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.</p>

<p>The post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists <a href="https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6719-9507">working with</a> the <a href="https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/hadza/">Hadza people</a> of Tanzania <a href="https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3225-5791">and with</a> the <a href="https://tsimane.anth.ucsb.edu/tsimaneinfo.html">Tsimane people</a> of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.</p>

<p>Insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality <a href="https://theconversation.com/britains-quarter-century-wealth-and-widening-inequality-287410">grows globally</a>. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over <a href="https://www.psypost.org/scientists-say-media-storm-around-myth-of-man-the-hunter-study-was-unjustified-and-misleading/">gender</a>, <a href="https://www.hbes.com/the-controversial-origins-of-war-and-peace/">war and peace</a> and whether humans are, <a href="https://aeon.co/essays/the-idea-of-primitive-communism-is-as-seductive-as-it-is-wrong">by nature, egalitarian</a> or <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2022.07.003">hierarchical</a>.</p>

<p>Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X25103932">more than a century of ethnography</a> to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="several children sit with a woman next to some harvested crops in front of a thatched hut" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763722/original/file-20261002-60-irns8e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People living in egalitarian societies like the Tsimane have similar, modest levels of material wealth.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Christopher von Rueden</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Is any society truly egalitarian?</h2>

<p>Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2801707">power, wealth and social status</a>. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.</p>

<p>Most families have similar, modest possessions and <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7259638">store little material wealth</a>. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12110-014-9213-4">how they can direct other people</a>. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.</p>

<p>While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers <a href="https://read.dukeupress.edu/ethnohistory/article-abstract/52/3/563/8552/Slavery-in-the-Greater-Lower-Columbia-Region">are very unequal</a> and that <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2801707">equality takes deliberate effort</a>, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.</p>

<p>A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had <a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374533229/theoriginsofpoliticalorder/">no permanent leadership and no hierarchy</a>, inequality only spread <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.ca/books/395860/the-spirit-level-new-edition-by-richard-wilkinsonkate-pickett/9780241954294">with the development of agriculture</a>, and humans are <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/humankind-9781408898956/">noble by nature</a>.</p>

<p>Some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, “<a href="https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/314162/the-dawn-of-everything-by-wengrow-david-graeber-and-david/9780141991061">The Dawn of Everything</a>,” calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies <a href="https://aeon.co/essays/not-all-early-human-societies-were-small-scale-egalitarian-bands">a scientific origin myth</a>.</p>

<p>So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.</p>



<h2>Inequality among hunter-gatherers</h2>

<p>In our recent wide-ranging <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X25103932">review of the evidence</a> from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.</p>

<p>Like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/anthropology/social-and-cultural-anthropology/kung-san-men-women-and-work-foraging-society?format=PB&amp;isbn=9780521295611">surrounding waterholes</a>. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they <a href="https://doi.org/10.3828/hgr.2015.2">bought, sold and hoarded ritual knowledge</a>. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3773591">hugely discriminating against orphans</a>.</p>

<p>Gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat <a href="https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/251032">exclusively for older men</a>, and give <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-hadza/paper">more respect to better hunters</a>. Across societies, women have universally <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2018.03.025">done more direct parenting</a>, and men have participated more frequently in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X25103932">community-level decision-making</a>.</p>

<p>No society lacks <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.leaqua.2018.09.001">informal leadership</a>. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/497672">power over the marriage choices of younger relatives</a>. </p>

<h2>Equality arises from self-interest</h2>

<p>Our study also found that although hunter-gatherers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2022.03.001">are frequently generous</a>, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status and autonomy. </p>

<p>A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf328">more taking than giving</a>, often through strongly stated <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/683021">demands or complaints</a>.</p>

<p>Another example is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12110-005-1000-9">ridicule and mockery</a> of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which <a href="https://libcom.org/article/egalitarian-social-organisation-among-hunter-gatherers-case-mbendjele-bayaka-jerome-lewis">keeps greed and bravado in check</a>. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status <a href="https://www.mpg.de/13772534/cooperation-with-high-status-individuals-may-increase-one-s-own-status">diffuses status throughout the community</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="semi circle of people outside facing a man squatting on the ground" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=575&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=575&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763723/original/file-20261002-50-rti63o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=575&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">The Tsimane reach decisions through community deliberation. Some have more influential voices than others, but everyone has the opportunity to contribute.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Christopher von Rueden</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Egalitarianism is alive and well</h2>

<p>Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.</p>

<p>Ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where <a href="https://www.vox.com/culture/23404571/china-vs-fandom-danmei-censorship-qinglang-social-media">governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech</a>. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04997-3">cooperation among people of different social strata</a>.</p>

<p>Like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today. </p>

<p>Egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289009/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

He is President of One Pencil Project (<a href="http://www.onepencilproject.org">www.onepencilproject.org</a>), a non-profit that funds educational opportunites for indigenous youth.</span></em></p></content>
    <summary>Hunter-gatherers do not always seek total equality, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t egalitarian.</summary>
    <author>
      <name>Duncan Stibbard Hawkes, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, Baylor University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/duncan-stibbard-hawkes-2748866"
excerpt: Even in egalitarian societies, people can be unequal in various ways
body: Even in egalitarian societies, people can be unequal in various ways
Duncan Stibbard Hawkes On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food
Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal – a kudu
He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas and heads home to enlist help
A kudu post-butchering, with portions going to various community members
Duncan Stibbard Hawkes News spreads like wildfire across the camp
They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more
Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still
On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less
People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share
It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality

But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies
Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives
Insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally

Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender , war and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical
So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are
People living in egalitarian societies like the Tsimane have similar, modest levels of material wealth
Christopher von Rueden Is any society truly egalitarian? Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth and social status
And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities
Most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth
When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people
People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort , the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy , inequality only spread with the development of agriculture , and humans are noble by nature
Some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals
The popular bestseller, “ The Dawn of Everything ,” calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance
Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth
So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between
Inequality among hunter-gatherers In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality

Like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes
The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold and hoarded ritual knowledge
The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans
The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men , and give more respect to better hunters
Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting , and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision-making
In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives
Equality arises from self-interest Our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous , the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity
Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status and autonomy
Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously
It can involve more taking than giving , often through strongly stated demands or complaints
Another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check

title: How did the Cornell rape case go so wrong?
excerpt: Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James at a news conference in New York City on October 2, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images In
body: Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James at a news conference in New York City on October 2, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images In October 2024, students at Cornell University received a campus crime alert about a reported sexual assault
Nearly two years later, on September 16, the victim, known only as “Jane Doe,” filed a civil lawsuit that brought national attention to her story

People across the country are asking what happened and why criminal charges never followed.  Doe alleges that seven men drugged and sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house two years ago

Her lawsuit also accuses the university, fraternity and sorority organizations, and a local bar of failing to protect her.  The lawyers for several of the men have denied the allegations and any wrongdoing
Cornell says its disciplinary actions led to suspensions and expulsions for some of the young men, and that the Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from campus
Doe went to campus police in November 2024, and the district attorney’s office reviewed her account and declined to bring charges
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said that what she described to Cornell police didn’t meet the state’s requirements for criminal charges
Van Houten reopened the investigation late last month while continuing to defend his original decision to not pursue charges , but it’s now out of his hands: On Thursday, New York Gov

Kathy Hochul named the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor to investigate the allegations, saying she had “lost faith” in Van Houten.  To break down why Van Houten didn’t pursue the case at the time and what should have happened instead, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Lauren Hersh , a former Brooklyn prosecutor who led the office’s sex trafficking unit and CEO of World Without Exploitation , about how authorities handled Jane Doe’s allegations, the limits of New York’s consent laws, and what needs to change.  Hersh also explains where she believes the case should go next and what a special prosecutor can do to investigate (the interview took place prior to James’s appointment)
Below is an excerpt of Hersh’s conversation with Noel edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
I want to start with what we know in 2024

A young woman who we know as “Jane Doe” goes to the Cornell campus police and says she had gone to a frat house while under the influence of alcohol.  At the frat house, she was given more alcohol and ketamine
Several men had sex with her while she was intoxicated
This is what she tells Cornell campus police
What, in your view, is supposed to happen next?  There are a number of things that could happen

What I would say about these cases is there is no perfect scenario of what is supposed to happen, because what is critically important is we listen to the desire of the survivor.  We want to take this at her pace
We want her to decide if she is ready to go forward, if she wants to speak to campus police, the Title IX office, if she wants to speak to the local law enforcement

There are a lot of variables here, but for me, what is critically important is that we’re listening to the survivor and what she ultimately wants to happen.  In the present day, the district attorney who was involved has said that his office reviewed Jane Doe’s statement at the time and found at the time that what she described didn’t meet the legal definition of a crime.  I think people want to understand, Lauren, how is that possible?  To be really candid with you, Noel, this is an area that seems super unclear to me because the role of the district attorney in that moment is to investigate.  When you first get a case file, you first get a victim statement, and especially with facts as horrific as these facts are, or our understanding of this six-page document that the DA read — I would never say that this is a clear-cut case where there’ll be a conviction at the end
What I can say with 100 percent certainty is if you get a document like that, as a prosecutor, that is a significant investigative lead
And so, as a prosecutor, what I believe to be good practice is starting to pull the layers back, trying to understand what transpired here

We now know that there are all these text messages that were shared between these boys, and the prosecutor’s now saying, “I didn’t know about the text messages.” It’s my understanding that there were a lot of boys on that particular text thread
And so a good investigator would have gone to that fraternity house and tried to interview some of those boys, tried to understand what were the contemporaneous statements made at that time

Were there any text messages? Was there any social media activity? And I believe that had they done that in a timely fashion, they likely would have come up with these text messages at that time and not two years later

What you’re saying is interesting because the DA has come out publicly and defended himself by saying, essentially, the details of this lawsuit, which was filed in September of this year, are different from the details in the young woman’s 2024 statement to the police.  He has used that in his defense, right? “Here’s what I knew at the time versus what this young woman is saying today.” I think I hear you saying that maybe that’s not an excuse? You’re asking about the inconsistent statements, and I find it troubling that the DA is leading with this notion that the victim has inconsistent statements because that feels to me like here we are making excuses and blaming the victim.  To my knowledge, the DA has not yet interviewed this victim
Perhaps he’s talking about the civil complaint, which I would think is written in a way where she has worked with her lawyer to put this together

And the initial statement, the initial six-page document that the DA read, my understanding is that it is basically a summary of a conversation.  Inconsistencies come in all shapes and sizes, so it’s hard to know exactly what we’re talking about here, but it is very common for there to be some inconsistencies

That is not a dealbreaker, despite the fact that this prosecutor wants the public to believe that it is.  What do you make of the prosecutor speaking publicly in the way that he is at this moment? I find it rather confusing

I’m not really understanding why he is doing a media tour rather than sitting in his office doing the work, interviewing this particular victim, interviewing witnesses, seeing what evidence actually exists
It seems to me that the DA has gotten to a conclusion before he’s done the work in actually investigating the case, and it is deeply troubling

And I think the governor should consider appointing a special prosecutor because I am not certain, based on this media tour, that this DA is able to give this particular survivor a full and fair investigation of the facts
Drugs and alcohol are central to this case, right? The young woman admits she had been drinking and she was using ketamine
Under New York law, how does that affect whether or not someone is believed to be capable of consenting to sex?  New York law is actually really problematic here
It’s a place where I believe we are desperate for a legislative fix

I think that there have been a lot of advocates who’ve been championing a correction to this voluntary intoxication loophole for a lot of years, and we’ve not been able to get it.  New York law makes it very, very hard to prosecute a person when the victim is voluntarily intoxicated, but not unconscious, and this new law would allow the prosecutors the ability to bring cases when the victim is so severely intoxicated but not physically helpless and where a reasonable person should have known the victim’s condition.  In this particular case, based on what we’re hearing, she was in a condition where a reasonable person should have known her condition
And so in this particular instance, the DA is right
This is a very, very hard case to prove in this moment, but I’m a big believer
We don’t not prosecute cases because they’re hard cases
But at the same time, we know that a change to the law is critically important.  You clearly want more investigation here

What questions do you want asked? Who do you want to be [interviewed]?  Before I say who and how and what that investigation looks like, I think it’s really important to say that when two years have passed and the DA did not investigate these cases immediately, we have a big problem on our hands
