Vonnegut responds News of what happened in Drake spread quickly in the press
Those who objected to the school board’s actions made comparisons to Nazi book burnings

The school district’s cause wasn’t helped by the fact that the superintendent’s last name was Fuhrman – evoking Adolf Hitler’s formal title, Führer – and the school board chairman’s last name was McCarthy, reminding the public of Joseph McCarthy , the disgraced anti-communist senator who sought to purge and censor Americans from all walks of life
Kurt Vonnegut objected to efforts to remove his works from school curricula
Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, photograph by Bernard Gotfryd When Kurt Vonnegut learned of the case, he was both angry and saddened

In a letter to the Drake school board, he insisted his books were “not sexy” and did not argue “in favor of wildness of any kind.” Instead, “they beg that people be kinder and more responsible than they often are.” He informed the board that he was a decorated World War II veteran who had fought against nations that hate books and burn them
The North Dakota incident, while the most egregious attempt to censor Vonnegut, was not the only case of its kind
As “Slaughterhouse-Five” made its way into high school and college curricula, it faced a backlash by parents and school boards who argued the novel was obscene and immoral
Its irreverent treatment of Christianity was deemed blasphemous, while its unsparing portrayal of the U.S. military’s bombing of Dresden, Germany, was condemned as anti-American

The book has been challenged as recently as January 2026, when the ACLU filed a lawsuit on behalf of Vonnegut’s estate after Utah’s “ sensitive materials law ” gave school districts a mechanism to ban the novel
The Supreme Court weighs in Censorship cases involving “Slaughterhouse-Five” are complex because they have occurred almost entirely in high schools rather than colleges
Schools must balance their responsibility to decide what material is appropriate for younger students with students’ First Amendment rights to receive information and ideas
One important case dealing with these issues made it all the way to the U.S

In 1976, several board members from the Island Trees School district in Long Island, New York, reacting to a list of “inappropriate” titles publicized by a conservative activist group, objected to 11 books held in the districts’ school libraries or included in the curriculum

Seven of the books were written by authors from minority ethnic or religious groups, including titles as seemingly inoffensive as “ Best Stories of Negro Writers ,” edited by Langston Hughes , and the young adult novel “ A Hero Ain’t Nothing but a Sandwich ” by Alice Childress

The 11th book on the list was “Slaughterhouse-Five.” At a press conference, school board member Frank Martin read excerpts from the novel out loud, focusing on a passage where one of Vonnegut’s characters, Kilgore Trout , reimagines the story of Christ’s crucifixion
Trout claims that this revised story actually offered a better moral than the original Gospel story: It teaches people to be kind to everyone, not just the well connected

Martin, however, declared that even if the rest of the book told the best story in the world, he wouldn’t want it in the school library “ with this stuff in it .” A woman wears a sticker produced by the Kurt Vonnegut Museum and Library in Indianapolis that proclaims ‘I Read Banned Books.’ Michael Blackshire/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Five high school students, led by 17-year-old Steven Pico, soon filed a lawsuit against the district, claiming the book removal was unconstitutional and that their First Amendment rights to freely receive information had been violated
The case wended its way through the lower courts for years, before it came to the Supreme Court in 1982
The justices wrote seven separate opinions and did not definitively settle the First Amendment issues
But a 5-4 majority did determine in favor of the students who argued that their case should have received a full trial rather than a summary judgment years ago
As the only Supreme Court case to date involving censorship in school libraries, Pico, while a limited ruling, did set out general guidelines still used today

The decision affirmed that school districts have the authority to supervise the education of students in their care and may remove materials that are, in the words of Justice William Brennan, “ pervasively vulgar ” or educationally unsuitable
But such a decision may not be based on a school district’s objections to the ideas expressed in the books

Books may not be removed on narrowly partisan or political grounds, and removal must comply with the “ transcendent imperatives of the First Amendment .” Book banning today Despite the fact that the justices ruled that books cannot be banned on partisan or political grounds, book banning has been on the rise in America since 2020
The literary and free speech advocacy group PEN America documented 2,532 instances of book bans in public schools in 2021–22
That figure rose to 3,362 in 2022–23 and nearly tripled to 10,046 in 2023–24
Since then, the numbers have dipped somewhat but are still alarmingly high
Surprisingly, many of the school censorship cases today still focus on the same old issues affecting “Slaughterhouse-Five” over 50 years ago – profanity, sexual content and violence

title: How Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is helping kids start reading when they’re very young

<title>How Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is helping kids start reading when they’re very young</title>
    <content type="html"><p>By the time <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/arts/music/dolly-parton-dead.html">Dolly Parton died on Aug. 25, 2026</a>, her <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/">Imagination Library</a> had gifted more than 332 million children’s books to babies and kids in all 50 states and <a href="https://theconversation.com/dolly-partons-imagination-library-what-its-success-means-for-childrens-reading-290977">four other countries</a>: Canada, the U.K., Australia and Ireland.</p>

<p>If they were set end to end, these books would circle the earth 1.8 times.</p>

<p>This free program mails an age-appropriate book monthly to each enrolled child from birth to age 5, meaning up to 60 books will fill these children’s shelves by the time they graduate from the program. </p>

<p>Though a selection committee tweaks the lists annually, each participant receives Watty Piper’s “<a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/series/DQR/the-little-engine-that-could/">The Little Engine That Could</a>” as their first book and Nancy Carlson’s “<a href="https://nancycarlson.com/look-out-kindergarten-here-i-come/">Look Out Kindergarten, Here I Come!</a>” as their last.</p>

<p>I’m an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Fe9cMqwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">information science professor who studies reading behavior</a>. In my research for an upcoming academic article about the Imagination Library, I’ve found that its free monthly books help families develop children’s literacy, prepare children for kindergarten and encourage a lifelong love of reading.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/tscb01jfukc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Dolly Parton describes her Imagination Library, starting with what inspired her to create it.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Emphasis on early literacy</h2>

<p>Parton, most remembered as a popular country singer, embraced <a href="https://rockhall.com/inductees/dolly-parton/">many musical genres</a> during her long and successful career in show business. She was also a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/nx-s1-5945081/dolly-parton-podcast">songwriter, entrepreneur, actor and philanthropist</a>.</p>

<p>She created this program because she, like most early childhood literacy experts, believed that reading <a href="https://naeducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/Anderson-Hiebert-Scott-Wilkinson-Becoming-a-Nation-of-Readers.pdf">begins in the home</a>. That is, parents and other guardians are a child’s first teachers, and reading aloud to children <a href="https://naeducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/Anderson-Hiebert-Scott-Wilkinson-Becoming-a-Nation-of-Readers.pdf">contributes to their future literacy</a>.</p>

<p>First graders who struggle with reading usually <a href="https://people.uncw.edu/kozloffm/learningtreadandwrite.pdf">continue to have trouble with literacy later on</a>.</p>

<p>Very young children in lower-income households generally <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0042085916654525">have less access to books</a> and hear <a href="https://products.brookespublishing.com/Meaningful-Differences-in-the-Everyday-Experience-of-Young-American-Children-P14.aspx">fewer words</a> than higher-income kids. This class-based difference may lead to <a href="https://products.brookespublishing.com/Meaningful-Differences-in-the-Everyday-Experience-of-Young-American-Children-P14.aspx">disparities in reading skills later on</a>.</p>

<h2>A homegrown program</h2>

<p>Like Parton, who was born in a <a href="https://www.visitmysmokies.com/blog/dolly-parton/dolly-partons-childhood-home/">one-bedroom cabin in an Appalachian region</a> of Tennessee that had neither running water nor electricity, the Imagination Library’s origins were modest. It started in her hometown, hardscrabble Sevier County, in late 1995. Its initial order of 1,760 books was destined for the children who lived where she grew up.</p>

<p>The program came from “a very serious place in my heart,” <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2016/06/02/dolly-parton-how-my-father-inspired-the-imagination-library.html">Parton once said</a>. On many occasions, she emphasized how her own father’s illiteracy inspired her to found it – with him.</p>

<p>“Daddy couldn’t read nor write, and it always just seemed to cripple him, and he was embarrassed about it,” <a href="https://americanlibrariesmagazine.org/2018/01/02/newsmaker-dolly-parton/">Parton told American Libraries in 2018</a>. “My daddy just loved it when all the little kids would call me ‘The Book Lady,’” <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/books/dolly-parton-imagination-library.html">she said later</a>.</p>

<p>In contrast, Parton <a href="https://archive.org/details/dollymylifeother00part">was a bookworm</a>. “I always loved books,” she <a href="https://www.chicagoreviewpress.com/dolly-on-dolly-products-9781641600040.php">explained in an interview</a>. “I don’t remember learning to read, it was just something I always did. That’s how I knew there was a world beyond the Smoky Mountains.”</p>



<h2>How it works</h2>

<p><a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/the-dollywood-foundation/">Parton’s Dollywood Foundation covers</a> overhead and administrative expenses, coordinates the book selection committee, maintains the book order system and arranges orders and fulfillment.</p>

<p>The Imagination Library is available to any child in a community participating in the program, regardless of their family’s income.</p>

<p>To be eligible, a community must secure a local partner. Local partners publicize the program and enroll children. They have to pay US$2.60 per month per child to defray costs of purchasing books wholesale and mailing them. These partners include schools, public libraries and government agencies, and several kinds of nonprofits, including foundations.</p>

<p>Nonpartisan expert committees of educators and librarians select the books, nearly all <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/usa/book-list/">published by Penguin Random House</a>.</p>

<p>The program is continuing under the direction of the Dollywood Foundation’s president, Jeff Conyers. A <a href="https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/by-topic/childrens/childrens-industry-news/article/101140-dolly-parton-s-children-s-literacy-legacy.html">Penguin Random House vice president said</a>, “We
will continue that work with the utmost pride and care, just as we know she would have wanted.”</p>

<p>But <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/books/dolly-parton-imagination-library.html">funding challenges</a> have arisen in at least four states. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

              <span class="caption">The Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum’s exhibit ‘Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker’ in 2025 included these three popular offerings from the Imagination Library.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-the-exhibit-on-display-at-the-opening-of-country-news-photo/2215993498?adppopup=true">Jason Kempin/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Steady growth and diversification</h2>

<p>By 2001, the Imagination Library had expanded to affiliates in nearly a dozen states. The next year, it extended its reach to <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/news-resources/year-in-review/">92 Native American communities</a>, partnering with the Cherokee Nation, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Parents as Teachers and the National Center for Family Literacy.</p>

<p>In late 2003, the Imagination Library <a href="https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/print/20040105/20408-parton-s-library-hits-one-million.html">mailed its one-millionth book</a>. In 2004, it launched its first statewide program – fittingly, in Tennessee. </p>

<p>It added <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/news-resources/year-in-review/">bilingual titles in Spanish and English</a> in 2003 and launched a bilingual Spanish website in 2022. The Imagination Library also supplied audio and braille books for those who needed them beginning in 2011.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/ed/2018/03/01/589912466/dolly-parton-gives-the-gift-of-literacy-a-library-of-100-million-books">Parton celebrated</a> when the library mailed its 100-millionth book in 2018. “We never thought it would be this big,” she told NPR. “I just wanted to do something great for my dad and for my home county and, at the most, maybe a couple of counties over. But then it just took wings of its own.”</p>

<p>The Imagination Library shipped its 200-millionth book in 2023 and its 300-millionth book in 2025. By 2024, <a href="https://imaginationlibrary.com/about-us/">1 in 7 children under the age of 5 in the United States</a> were receiving books for free every month, courtesy of this initiative. </p>

<p>Other programs give free books to young children, including <a href="https://reachoutandread.org/">Reach Out and Read</a> in the U.S., which since 1989 has handed them out at children’s medical checkups. <a href="https://www.booktrust.org.uk/">Bookstart</a>, which launched in 1992, offers every baby in England, Wales and Northern Ireland a free book and tips on reading aloud to kids.</p>

<h2>Program benefits</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-016-0815-9">Parents and caregivers</a>
 <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">highly</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2023.2202179">praise</a> the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02568543.2024.2322731">program</a>.</p>

<p>Many studies have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00094056.2012.699850">children get excited about getting</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">their own books</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2023.2202179">in the mail</a>, addressed to them personally. Both they and their families also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00094056.2012.699850">take great pride in book</a> <a href="https://coloradolab.org/2025/08/13/evaluation-report-imagination-library-of-colorado/">ownership</a>.</p>

<p>“A lot of (children) wait at the mailbox at the first of the month,” Parton <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2000/03/23/the-reliable-source/9f3f768d-ea9f-4801-9252-45cb4e61ea5c/">told The Washington Post</a>. “They think that I bring the book myself, like I’m Santa Claus.”</p>

<p>As one parent <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">told an education researcher</a>, “We read the books when they come in the mail instead of watching TV.”</p>

<p>The library’s books “<a href="https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320922140">nudge</a>” children to make reading a regular habit. Many studies have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-016-0815-9">children who are read</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">to more frequently</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02568543.2024.2322731">by</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2023.2202179">their loved</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/09575146.2021.1908234">ones</a>, spend more time <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02568543.2024.2322731">reading together daily</a> and ask more frequently for books to be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">read to them</a>.</p>

<p>This program aims not only to boost a child’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-016-0815-9">love of reading</a> but to improve their cognitive development and get them ready for elementary school by enlarging their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244016669973">vocabulary and improving their listening skills</a>.</p>

<p>Kids who get the books tend to know more letters, understand how books and printed words work, recognize and retain words’ sounds, and both <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03004430.2026.2678212">understand and use more spoken words</a>. Similarly, <a href="https://coloradolab.org/2025/08/13/evaluation-report-imagination-library-of-colorado/">children enrolled in the program have scored higher</a> than their peers when they take a standard kindergarten entrance early-reading skills test.</p>

<p>In line with Parton’s original goal, the Imagination Library may do the most to change reading habits in <a href="https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320922140">lower-income homes</a> – where children’s books tend to be scarce.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292207/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Anthropic’s Christopher Olah shakes hands with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on May 25, 2026. | Alberto Pizzoli / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Hi readers, happy Friday! It’s been a big week for the AI debate — not the one about whether it will cause the robot apocalypse, though there’s still plenty to worry about there, but instead about whether the technology is conscious.  The folks at Anthropic, the AI company behind the large language model Claude, certainly seem to think it is — or at least, they’re extremely open to the possibility.  As the New York Times reported earlier in the week, the company has spent the last year grappling with the question by speaking with religious thinkers from many faith traditions in an effort to chart a moral course for the LLM (that is, to keep it from killing us all, so maybe it is all one big debate).  In the process, the Times reports, some of those thinkers observed that members of the Anthropic team were “relating to [Claude] like a conscious being” and even, according to it, a degree of “moral status.”  On the flip side of this debate is Pope Leo XIV, who decidedly does not seem to buy into AI consciousness arguments
His “Magnifica Humanitas” encyclical earlier this year argued that AI will never be able to replace humanity — and reportedly “alarmed” Anthropic’s co-founder, Christopher Olah

Since then, Pope Leo has continued to emphasize the differences between humans and machines this week. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others,” he posted on Friday. “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.” Loneliness machines Conscious or no (and that’s a no from me), it’s hard to argue that tech companies don’t want you to interact with their models like people

That includes OpenAI and Meta, both of whom introduced “cute” new AI agents — called Dots and Muse, respectively — last month.  As my colleague Adam Clark Estes reported this week , though, the promise of a companionable, always-there AI might not be the best idea in the world — especially for children

A new study, still under review, suggests that AI use may be causing loneliness in middle schoolers.  Adam spoke with the lead researcher on the study, UNC Chapel Hill professor Anne Maheux, who  explained that “middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time.”  According to Maheux, one big point where AI chatbots fail compared to human beings is “friction,” or the complicated push-and-pull dynamic of any connection with a real human being

By contrast, chatbots are “sycophantic, highly agreeable, anthropomorphized,” she says, which can lead to kids “developing expectations or understandings of interactive relationships that are actually fundamentally at odds with a normal human relationship.” People, in other words, still matter, no matter how much the AI companies want us to build our lives around machines instead

title: The Cornell case, explained
excerpt: Kathy Hochul asked on Friday , “would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while she was intoxicated by five men in a frate
body: Kathy Hochul asked on Friday , “would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while she was intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?”  Hochul was speaking about the case of a former Cornell student who said she was raped by several members of the university’s Chi Phi fraternity in 2024
At the time, the district attorney filed no criminal charges
The case has rocked the nation and forced a renewed reckoning over how sexual assault is dealt with in higher education

While the district attorney has defended his handling of the case , many politicians and legal experts are now examining whether certain details of the alleged victim’s account were neglected, and prosecutors have reopened the case
Amy Wang is a staff reporter at the Washington Post who’s been covering the story over the past week

She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about what allegedly happened on the night in question, what happened afterward, and what we still don’t know.  Since the two spoke, New York state Attorney General Letitia James has also been assigned to oversee the case and said it is now “an active criminal investigation.” As new information comes to light, further legal action could be taken
Below is an excerpt of the conversation between King and Wang, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
In October of 2024, a young woman went to a fraternity house near Cornell University’s campus
Who is this young woman, and why did she go to the frat house that night? The young woman is only identified in documents as Jane Doe, so we don’t know her name

And around 11 pm on the night of October 19, 2024, this Jane Doe goes to a bar on campus, and then, after that, goes to the Chi Phi fraternity house to hang out with a friend.  She said that she was already pretty intoxicated at that point, and she’d had maybe 10 drinks in about three hours
Her friend at the fraternity house hands her a beer
After that is where she alleges that another member of the fraternity pressured her into taking drugs, specifically ketamine and marijuana, and drinking more alcohol
She alleges that two members of the fraternity assaulted her, and that one of them later sent a Snapchat message out to active Chi Phi members
The message is pretty graphic, but essentially invites them to join in, and several did
In about three weeks, this young woman was going to go to the Cornell campus police and report what happened that night

But in the interim, what was going on? What was happening? We now know, based on reporting by the New York Times and CBS News, this young woman was a member of a campus sorority, so she went to a member of her sorority and was trying to make sense of what happened

She wasn’t using, according to their reporting, the word “rape” or “assault.” And she was also seeing rumors circulating around campus about what had taken place at the fraternity house and was growing concerned about how they portrayed her
She, in the interim, also received a text message from one of the seven men at the fraternity essentially apologizing for how things went down the other night

She is not yet accusing them of assault, but is chatting, even seeks to reassure him in that first message.  On October 22, she then makes an appointment at the campus health clinic because she had what she thought was a UTI and wanted to be tested because she told the doctor that she had gone through a traumatic experience.  According to the New York Times reporting , you could see her thinking about what happened kind of evolve over those few weeks
She at some point says that this is starting to ruin her life, and she’s sleeping and crying and she’s feeling ashamed
She’s just really grappling with what had taken place, trying to make sense of it
By November 3 is when, according to these investigative documents that were obtained by the Times, she kind of comes to this conclusion that what happened at the party at Chi Phi was assault
She texts one of the seven fraternity members and says, “This was not consensual
I was given more ketamine than I can remember,” and that she was uncomfortable
A few days later, November 7th, 2024, according to these documents, she goes to the ER and asks for a rape kit
And the following day is when she goes to Cornell University Police

When she goes to the police, how does she characterize what happened to the police? What does she tell them? What she tells the police is that she believes she was assaulted, and she tells the police that it had started out as something that was consensual

And then at the end she says, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.” She tells police she was extremely uncomfortable and that she kept taking ketamine in part because she thought she might black out and pass out
She had thought of at least two of the men as her friends
After the events of that night, she is then confronted with rumors that were spreading across campus, sort of depicting her as loose and blaming her essentially
What happens after Jane Doe talks to the police? What do they do? When she talks to Cornell University Police, they summarize what she said in a six-page statement that she then signs
And that is the statement that is submitted to the Tompkins County district attorney
And the district attorney would be the person who would bring charges or decide not to bring charges
What does he decide?  Yes, so the district attorney decides not to bring charges in 2024 based on, he has said, the sworn statement that she signs to police.  The DA says no charges for the seven men
Were they disciplined in any way? We don’t know exactly how each of the men were disciplined
Cornell has said that they faced a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions and suspensions
One of the details that had gone particularly viral about this is that the disciplinary measures included for some of the students to write essays
Cornell has not denied that, but it has specifically denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure

The university has cited privacy laws and said it really can’t release any more specifics about how individual students were punished or not punished.  What did Jane Doe do after first talking to the police and then learning the DA wasn’t going to press charges? After she goes to police, we know she remains on campus and she has to continue seeing some of these men

title: AI found a way to make middle school worse
excerpt: There’s a lot to be anxious about as AI agents and bots get more integrated into every aspect of our lives
body: There’s a lot to be anxious about as AI agents and bots get more integrated into every aspect of our lives

Meta, which recently agreed to pay over $17 billion to settle a lawsuit related to harming kids , now wants you to hand over all your online accounts to an inexplicably cute “agent” named Muse that might give a stranger your home address
OpenAI just introduced little blobs called Dots that can supposedly automate routine tasks , like planning dinner and ordering it from your favorite neighborhood spot
AI companies don’t just want you to talk to their chatbots; they want their agents to be an indispensable part of your daily routine
As a parent, however, I think that perhaps the worst thing AI could do is be my kid’s friend.  AI companions have been around longer than ChatGPT , and they’re growing in popularity with young users

More than half of teens have interacted with AI companions at least a few times a month, and one in three decided to talk about a serious issue with AI companions instead of real people, according to a Common Sense Media survey conducted last year
In certain groups and situations, a chatbot could offer some benefit — a lifeline for, say, LGBTQ youth who don’t have any in-person support networks, one study found
But even so, there are important caveats and risks

Meanwhile, other experts are telling parents never to let their kids access AI companions , warning them that these chatbots have a history of offering dangerous advice and engaging in sexualized conversations
Sixteen-year-old Adam Raine died by suicide last April after developing a relationship and discussing his plans with ChatGPT
If you have kids, these are horrifying stories to hear
It’s reasonable to wonder how widespread the issues are, and who they are affecting most
As of right now, the majority of younger kids aren’t using AI for companionship (phew!)

But for those who are, where do the issues arise? And how do they go from using ChatGPT for help with their homework to opening up to it about their problems to preferring it to their human friends?  Some answers are starting to emerge from research.  Why I wrote this My first daughter was born not long after ChatGPT hit the scene, and as someone who’s covered tech for years, I knew the technology’s effects would be profound, especially for young people
So when I came across Anne Maheux’s study on middle schools and AI companions, I had to know more about how things are going
For even young adolescents, there’s a direct link between AI companion use and mental health issues, according to a new study by researchers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

Their paper, which is still under review, is the first longitudinal study in the US that has looked at the bidirectional association between AI companionship in adolescents and mental health issues, according to one of the researchers
It charted AI use among 2,300 middle schoolers and found that about one in five used AI for emotional companionship

Those who used AI more reported higher levels of loneliness. “It’s not just that the lonely kids are using AI, and they’re otherwise unharmed,” said Anne Maheux , an assistant professor of psychology and neuroscience at UNC Chapel Hill and the lead author on the study. “It is that using AI comes first, and middle school students are increasing their sense of loneliness following the use of AI.” I recently spoke to Maheux about her research and the role of technology in young people’s lives
We discussed how much parents and teachers know about what is going on, what kids get out of human relationships that AI can’t provide, and whether she’d let a child under her care use an AI chatbot

While she said there is a lot to be scared of right now, there is some evidence that, when designed with the intention of promoting child learning and development and under the supervision of a caring adult, AI can offer some benefits, and, ultimately, she’s optimistic that we can design a better future for kids.  The conversation below has been lightly edited for length and clarity

How do so many kids end up with an AI companion? Do kids start using AI for homework help and end up in an emotional relationship with the technology?  At a high level, AI companions — in our darkest vision of what that might look like — would be a kid calling an AI chatbot their best friend
There are certainly plenty of kids who are experiencing that, but it’s not to say that it’s all kids or even most kids
I think that’s good news.  But it’s also true that the line between opening up AI to ask a question about your homework and a full-blown AI companionship relationship involves a lot of gray areas

There’s evidence, mostly preliminary and anecdotal evidence, to suggest that very few people open up to AI with the primary initial goal of developing an intimate friendship or relationship.  Most people open it out of a curiosity, sense of novelty, or seeking an answer to a question that’s very pragmatic
Then that can potentially evolve into something more akin to seeking personal advice or help making a decision or help making sense of one’s recent experiences with other humans
And that can potentially evolve to something that’s a bit more emotional
What did your latest study on adolescents, AI companions, and mental health reveal? Some kids seek out AI for certain purposes in different ways than other kids

For some kids, AI companionship is particularly attractive, especially the kids who maybe don’t have close friends or social networks in their offline life and who are already lonely.  It’s a chicken-and-egg problem

Is it that these kids are seeking out AI companions or is it that having an AI companion is exacerbating those potential vulnerabilities or exacerbating risk for mental health problems? What we found is that interacting with an AI companion in a way that’s akin to emotional intimacy among middle school students is longitudinally associated with increases over time in loneliness

So the kids who are seeking out these companions, who are presumably already lonely, are also experiencing an increase in loneliness over time.  There is this potential directionality question that we’re starting to answer here: It’s not just that the lonely kids are using AI, and they’re otherwise unharmed
It is that using AI comes first, and middle school students are increasing their sense of loneliness following the use of AI
In other words, middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time

Do you have a sense of how often these kids are using the chatbots?  In our sample — so again, these are US middle school kids — about 15 to 20 percent say that they’re using it at least a few times a week for any purpose
We don’t have specific rates of use for companionship because the questions that we asked were just not framed in a frequency measure, but more in how emotionally intimate they felt with the chatbot
What else could have been causing that loneliness? There are almost definitely many causes, and I think that our data suggests that AI companionship may be one cause

I’m a scientist and trying to be hesitant about these things, but the reality is that whether or not AI use causes loneliness in this particular case, there are definitely other things that are also causing loneliness.  That could be a myriad of things about the kid, maybe they have a lot of social anxiety, maybe they struggle with social skills, maybe the kid has had struggles in their family life and doesn’t have a strong sense of connection and belonging at home
The kid just doesn’t have enough access to appropriate resources

So certainly there’s other things that are at play here, and typically technology use is one of many factors that can influence a kid’s mental health.  And how much do you think that parents and teachers know about what’s going on, and how well-equipped do you think they are to intervene or to just be more involved in how these kids are using this technology?  It’s a very slippery technology
The way kids are using it has changed rapidly in just the last year or two years

title: An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
excerpt: Mind-reading, but make it science: Researchers at the Weizmann Institute have built an AI tool that reconstructs images people are looking at—just from their br
body: Mind-reading, but make it science: Researchers at the Weizmann Institute have built an AI tool that reconstructs images people are looking at—just from their brain scans—with striking accuracy

A smarter decoder: The tool uses two AI branches—one tracking image structure, one tracking content—and cleverly trains itself on images never shown to real people, meaning it needs just one hour of brain scan data per person instead of the usual 40

Big promise, bigger questions: Scientists are excited about potential uses—helping paralyzed people communicate, decoding dreams, studying PTSD—but warn that as the technology moves toward consumer EEG devices, the risk of extracting someone's thoughts without consent becomes uncomfortably real. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145588" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and re-create that image with remarkable precision

It can go the other way, too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.  In the image above, for example, the left-hand image of each pair is what the user actually saw—and its right-hand counterpart is what the model reconstructed from the brain scan.   Michal Irani, who developed the tool with her colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, hopes her “mind-reading” tool will ultimately reveal more about how the brain works, and could perhaps be used to help locked-in people communicate, or allow scientists to re-create the content of dreams.  Judy Illes, a neuroethicist and professor of neurology at the University of British Columbia in Canada, who was not involved in the research, describes the work as “magnificent.” “The idea [of using this approach] to help people with neurologic conditions … therapeutically is tremendously exciting,” she says

But other scientists warn that a similar approach could be used to reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent. “The results seem very impressive,” says Tommy Sprague, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But if there’s a way to surreptitiously extract information about what you’re thinking about, then …150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways.” Peeking into the brain Neuroscientists have been working for years on ways to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to reconstruct what people see and what’s going on in their minds
The first attempts produced images that were blurry and hard to make sense of
Advances in technology—both in the fMRI scans themselves and in the tools used to make sense of the results—have led to improvements over the years
Irani and her colleagues started by analyzing publicly available brain-scan data

Other researchers had already collected scans from volunteers who were shown hundreds of images while they lay in fMRI scanners. fMRI uses a giant magnet to track the flow of oxygenated blood through the brain
Brain areas that “light up” on the scans are thought to be those that are particularly active at any given moment
The results are not especially specific—in typical fMRI scanners, a highlighted “voxel” of activity covers around three cubic millimeters
Each cubic millimeter contains around 16,000 neurons
But Irani and her colleagues used newer datasets collected using scanners with a higher resolution—each voxel covered around one cubic millimeter of neurons, she says
Those datasets showed what the brain activity of volunteers looked like when they viewed various images
Other teams have done this too, and several other tools have been used to re-create images from brain-scan data

These models can generate an image of a banana, but it would look different, she says. “It wouldn’t have the same structure, the same position.” A better decoder The researchers wanted to more closely re-create the images that had been seen
The first step was to train an AI model on already available data from eight people who each had been shown around 9,000 images while in a high-resolution fMRI scanner

Crucially, their “brain decoder” has two branches—one to predict the structure of an image (where the colors are, for instance) and a second to predict its content (for example, a bunch of bananas on a plate)

The predictions allow a diffusion model , a type of AI best known for creating video and images by gradually cleaning up a noisy mess of pixels, to produce a much more accurate representation of what the person saw

But to improve the models they needed more data—far more than was actually available.   To get around this problem, Irani and her colleagues trained another model—an encoder that can predict brain activity from an image
The team then used the encoder and decoder together to improve both tools
It works like this: Start with a new image of, say, a leopard
Then use the encoder to predict what someone’s fMRI brain scan would look like when the person saw that picture
The decoder is then used to reconstruct the image
At first, the reconstruction probably won’t look much like a leopard, says Irani
But repeatedly training the models this way eventually leads to dramatic improvements
This approach also allows the team to train their models on as many images as they want, even images that have never been shown to a person in an fMRI scanner
Irani says that around 70% of the training data is from images that were not originally paired with fMRI scans
By combining data from multiple studies, they were also able to identify brain regions that seem to share functions across all individuals
One region seemed to respond to images of food, for example, while another responded to images of sports

Irani, a computer scientist, says she is now working with neuroscientists “to see if we can actually use these tools that we’ve developed to really find out new things about the brain.” The resulting “universal brain encoder” can work on a scan from a new person with minimal calibration
In other attempts, a tool has typically required about 40 hours of fMRI data on anyone new before it can be used to predict what that person is seeing
Irani’s decoder only needs one hour of data, she says
The finding was presented at the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience conference in New York last month

That could make it valuable for neuroscientists studying the brain, says Sprague. “None of us can afford 40 hours of imaging for a new subject,” he says. “It’s something like $600 to $1,000 an hour.” Tools like this one could speed up research, he says
State of the art The encoder and decoder aren’t perfect. “Of course we have failures,” says Irani

Over a Zoom call, she pointed out an image of a cake that her tool reconstructed as a pile of three sandwiches, and another of a dog in a bathtub that was reconstructed as a similarly colored goat in a bathtub

In a comparison test, the tool was found to be much better than previously described ones. “All in all, really we outperformed the others by a significant margin,” Irani says. “Mind reading” is a “cute, jazzy name” for what they’re doing, she adds
Irani is now planning to move beyond images to video and audio

She wants to be able to reconstruct what people are thinking about or imagining, and the contents of their dreams. “That’s something we don’t have yet,” she says. “But we’re striving to achieve it.” Such a tool might enable people who are “locked in” and completely paralyzed to communicate using their brain activity alone, she says

body: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”

body: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders
